summary: Research the self-grading verify-and-retry loop idea: codebase fit + market/competitive, adversarially verified

codebase_findings: REFUTED IDEA CLAIM: the roadmap label that max_review_fix_cycles is 'validated-but-unused' / 'no code path consumes it' is FALSE. It is already wired to a live reviewer->fixer circuit-breaker: review_fix_cycle_limit_reached (src/app/mod.rs:3704-3710) reads self.config.limits.max_review_fix_cycles and compares against review_fix_cycle_count (src/app/mod.rs:6019-6033, counts reviewer->fixer transitions); stop_for_review_fix_cycle_limit (src/app/mod.rs:3712-3724) halts with RunState::LimitReached + a run_limit_reached event keyed 'max_review_fix_cycles'. Enforced from both decision paths: handle_single_agent_decision (src/app/mod.rs:1977-1980) and handle_parallel_group_decision (src/app/mod.rs:1993-1998). Covered end-to-end by review_fix_cycle_limit_stops_before_extra_fixer_pass (src/app/mod.rs:11391) and unit test review_fix_cycle_count_skips_initial_fixer_pass (src/app/mod.rs:11321).

TRUE GAP (the actual kernel of the feature): what does NOT exist is an automatic self-grading loop that programmatically grades a just-completed step and re-dispatches the SAME agent with the critique. The existing cycle is orchestrator-DISCRETIONARY (the LLM chooses to route reviewer then fixer), not auto-injected after an Edit. Roadmap refs: docs/feature-roadmap.md:148-151, plans/AUDIT-and-ROADMAP-2026-06-14.md:326.

max_review_fix_cycles is type Limit (enum Value(u32)|Unlimited) at src/config/mod.rs:178, default Limit::Value(2) at :190; semantics is_reached_by uses value>=limit (src/config/mod.rs:74-99). The LimitVisitor rejects 0 (src/config/mod.rs:131-135), so max_review_fix_cycles=0 fails to parse; minimum effective value is 1. No dedicated/cross-field validation exists for limits (validators at :1749-1798 only cover models/env/runtime args).

Council is the existing virtual-routing-target template a grader sentinel would copy. Sentinel const COUNCIL_WORKFLOW_AGENT_ID='council' (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:9). Validation short-circuits the real agent lookup in validate_agent_reference (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:637-670) before config.agents.get(). VERIFICATION CAVEAT: dispatch, execution, and synthesis all live in src/app/mod.rs (drive loop), NOT in src/orchestrator/ — the orchestrator module only VALIDATES the virtual id and emits a prompt routing line (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:700-723). Dispatch branch: handle_single_agent_decision src/app/mod.rs:1960; executor run_council_workflow src/app/mod.rs:3155-3323; synthesis synthesize_council_decision src/app/mod.rs:5557-5626 + council_agent_result :5628-5699.

There is NO generic virtual-target registry: council is hardcoded `if agent_id == COUNCIL_WORKFLOW_AGENT_ID` string-equality at 3 sites (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:642 validation, src/app/mod.rs:1960 dispatch, src/orchestrator/mod.rs:704 prompt). A grader sentinel would replicate this bespoke shape (new const + validation branch + dispatch branch + prompt line + executor/synthesis fns), not plug into an extension point — so 'clean reuse' is a template-copy, not a plugin seam.

AgentResult struct is at src/orchestrator/mod.rs:147-160 (idea's cite of 154-158 points at individual fields). It has NO machine-parsable pass/fail verdict field. The only machine verdict is status: AgentResultStatus (enum Completed/Blocked/Failed/Cancelled/ParseError/LimitReached/ApprovalDenied/NoChanges, src/orchestrator/mod.rs:124-135), which carries OPERATIONAL meaning (NoChanges, ApprovalDenied), not a quality judgment. findings/verification/blocker (Vec<String>/Option<String>) are free-text SELF-attested by the agent's JSON contract (parse_agent_result :297-299; schema brief src/runtime/codex.rs:320-333, duplicated in claude.rs/cursor.rs). 'verification' is the agent grading ITSELF, so it cannot serve as an external verdict. A clean grader contract needs a NEW field/schema.

Capability enum is at src/config/mod.rs:26-37 (idea hinted actions/mod.rs, which only defines ActionKind/ToolName + the mapping). Capability::Verify and Capability::Review are NON-gating — only Read/Command/Edit map to harness actions (src/config/mod.rs:64-71, src/actions/mod.rs:702-709). A grader profile needs Read (+Command to run real checks) and must NOT have Edit; Verify/Review only shape orchestrator routing guidance (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:766-780) and decision validation (:661-668).

An existing grader-shaped profile already ships: built-in reviewer (enabled by default) has caps Read/Command/Verify/Review, no Edit, instructions 'risk-first review of completed work ... do not edit files' (src/config/mod.rs:837-855, DEFAULT_REVIEWER_INSTRUCTIONS :669-675). fixer is Read/Edit/Command/Verify (:817-836). So a grader could be the reviewer profile (or a clone with a strict verdict contract).

Primary auto-grader interception point: the AgentResult arm of run_agent_step at src/app/mod.rs:3083-3094, where the producing agent's profile is already in scope (fetched at :3052), so one can check agent.has_capability(&Capability::Edit) + result.changed_files non-empty before pushing RunStepResult::Agent onto run.previous_results. Note run_agent_step returns AgentStepOutcome::Completed even when result.status is Blocked/Failed — 'step completed' means 'agent produced a result', not 'work succeeded'. Whole-run completion is a separate orchestrator call (DecisionStatus::Complete -> RunState::Completed at src/app/mod.rs:1927).

Per-step limit duplication CONFIRMED but recounted: the fully-duplicated set-state+run_limit_reached-event+return block for max_agent_steps appears 4x (src/app/mod.rs:2399, 2895, 3040, 3208), with a 5th predicate call at :3772; the broader per-step time/action re-checks span 6 distinct methods (9 step-time stop sites, 2 step-action). Dedicated stop_for_* helpers exist for every OTHER limit (wall-clock :3648, step-time :3666, step-action :3685, review-fix :3712, parallel-group :2357) but NOT for per-step max_agent_steps. A naive grader step widens this to a 5th/6th copy unless refactored first.

Events are stringly-typed: HistoryEvent.kind is a free-form String (src/history/mod.rs:12-26); there is no enum registry. record_event/record_event_with_group (src/app/mod.rs:4164-4241) is the single chokepoint (durable JSONL append + chat projection feed + state publish). The projection dispatch (src/app/chat/projection.rs:58-111) has a catch-all `_ => {}` at :110, so a new 'grade_round' kind is durably persisted but INVISIBLE in chat until an apply_* arm is added. Precedent asymmetry: step_limit_reached events have no projection arm (invisible) while run_limit_reached IS projected.

WaitingForUser is a reusable pause/resume transport but currently has NO accept/retry/abort routing. Pause: handle_orchestrator_decision WaitingForUser arm captures the full RunDriveContext into pending_clarification, mints a question_id, records clarification_requested (src/app/mod.rs:1895-1926). Resume: resolve_pending_clarification (src/app/mod.rs:1689-1736) just APPENDS the answer to run.prompt and re-drives the orchestrator — there is no branch interpreting a tri-state choice. Today exhausted grade cycles hard-stop (RunState::LimitReached) rather than escalating, so user escalation is a behavior change at one site (stop_for_review_fix_cycle_limit).

Rendering N grade/retry rounds as ONE evolving chat item requires a stable ChatLifecycleKey shared across rounds (new GradeCycle{run_id} variant or reuse Run{run_id}) plus an apply_grade_round arm that accumulates cumulative body lines itself (upsert replaces in place, src/app/chat/projection.rs:1339-1383), capped by MAX_BODY_LINES=12 (:19). Council is the cautionary counter-example: it does NOT collapse — each councillor is a separate Step item and council markers are keyless diagnostics (lifecycle_key:None).
market_findings: The idea's framing that 'a built-in critic loop is exactly the self-correction larger agent frameworks charge for' is LARGELY FALSE/imprecise. Two realities: (1) every major OSS framework gives the loop away free as an assemble-it-yourself primitive (LangGraph reflection/reflexion, CrewAI guardrails+retry, AutoGen/AG2 critic agent, MS Agent Framework LLM-as-judge, OpenAI Agents SDK guardrails); (2) paid products (Devin, Cursor BugBot, Qodo) bundle the loop into a whole product and charge for compute/packaging (cloud VMs, autofix, ensemble validation, observability), never itemizing the loop as a gated SKU. No one sells 'a critic loop' standalone.

CrewAI task guardrails are the closest prior art to the proposed design and are free/OSS: a guardrail validates output right after the agent finishes (function-based or LLM/natural-language) and on failure routes the error message back to the SAME agent to retry, with a configurable retry cap (~2 extra attempts by default). This is almost exactly 'grader judges pass/fail, re-run same agent with critique appended, bounded by max cycles'.

Built-in self-correction is becoming TABLE STAKES, not a USP. Claude Code 2.1 (the harness's direct competitor) promotes auto-verification to a native workflow: generate -> run lint/type/test -> evaluate vs pass criteria -> self-correct/retry/confirm. Community patterns add a fresh-model verification SUBAGENT and Stop/PostToolUse hooks gating completion. Cursor and Devin ship automatic run-and-fix loops bundled in the product.

Two productized monetization lines exist around grading: (1) eval/LLM-as-judge platforms sold to AI builders (DeepEval/Confident AI, Braintrust, Galileo, Evidently, LangSmith, Arize, Ragas); (2) in-product reviewers/verifiers sold to developers (Cursor BugBot, Qodo, Greptile, Devin). A self-grading critic loop sits at their intersection as an INTERNAL verifier, not a separable product.

Re-running the SAME agent that was graded is a known weak spot. Claude Code's verification subagent and AG2's critic deliberately use a SEPARATE/fresh-context model to grade so the worker isn't its own judge. atelier already separates grader (reviewer) from implementer, which is the right instinct — but the design must ensure the grader is a distinct agent/context, not implementer self-grading.

Unbounded self-correction is a documented, expensive failure mode: Devin users report the agent 'gets stuck in expensive loops, racking up compute while failing to deliver working code', and LangGraph reflexion makes the max-cycle termination an explicit conditional edge. This validates the proposed bounded-cycle guardrail (which atelier already has via max_review_fix_cycles) as core, not an afterthought.

Market demand for automated code verification is real and growing: AI-generated code now ~46% of new code, turning human-only review into a bottleneck, and rework costs are rising sharply post-AI-adoption — the concrete pain a verify loop targets. But the credible value story must tie the grade to external signals (compile/test/lint), the very signals that demonstrably work.

Economics favor a per-step grader IF it cuts rework: a single LLM-judge pass costs ~$0.001-0.003 (GPT-4o-mini) to ~$0.015-0.045 (Claude Sonnet), far below the $30-40/dev/mo willingness-to-pay seen for in-product reviewers (Cursor BugBot ~$40 add-on, Qodo ~$30). Verifier reranking research shows higher accuracy at lower k than self-consistency using 1-3x fewer tokens, and Self-Truncation Best-of-N matches full Best-of-N at 75-80% lower cost — so a bounded single verification pass is a small, tunable multiplier.
differentiators: Automatic-by-default + opinionated + bounded is the honest differentiator: convenience/batteries-included UX, NOT unlocking a paywalled capability. OSS frameworks make you assemble the loop; atelier would ship it wired and config-bounded out of the box. Position it as that, not as 'what others charge for'.

atelier ALREADY structurally separates grader (reviewer, Read/Command/Verify/Review, no Edit) from implementer (fixer, has Edit), avoiding the same-agent self-grading bias that plagues naive reflection loops — provided the grader runs in a distinct agent/context. Most OSS examples and CrewAI default to re-running the SAME agent, so a clean grader/implementer split is a genuine (if modest) edge.

The defensible design — and the one the evidence demands — grounds the grade in EXTERNAL execution (compile/test/lint), not pure LLM self-grade. atelier already has the primitives: Capability::Command + the RunCommand action let a grader actually run tests and feed real failure locators back. Few terminal harnesses make external-signal grounding a first-class, config-driven default; that, not the loop pattern itself, is where atelier can stand apart.

atelier already owns the bounding guardrail infrastructure (max_review_fix_cycles wired live, RunState::LimitReached, cycle-count loop detection) that competitors had to bolt on — so it can ship a converging, non-runaway loop without new safety machinery, only new routing.

SKEPTICAL NOTE: 'terminal-native, single-binary, config-driven' are real atelier traits but are NOT loop-specific differentiators — every coding agent now ships some self-verify loop (Claude Code 2.1, Cursor, Devin, Cline). The loop alone is commoditized; the only durable edge is (a) external-signal grounding by default, (b) clean grader/implementer separation, and (c) bounded+observable cycles surfaced transparently in the TUI transcript.

stats: Reflexion (arXiv:2303.11366, NeurIPS 2023): ~8% absolute boost from self-reflection over an episodic-memory baseline; 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs 80% GPT-4 baseline — but feedback is EXTERNAL (unit tests / env reward), not pure self-grade.
Self-Refine (arXiv:2303.17651): ~20% average improvement over single-pass across 7 tasks (GPT-3.5/ChatGPT/GPT-4); gains plateau fast and depend on critique specificity, not round count.

CRITIC (arXiv:2305.11738, ICLR 2024): pure self-evaluation verifies its own answers at only ~54% on HotpotQA (near random) and self-critique scored WORSE than the original output on TriviaQA — tool feedback is what drives correction.

Self-Preference Bias (arXiv:2410.21819): LLMs (GPT-4 strongest) over-rate their own outputs vs humans; measured self-preference roughly -38% to +90% on ArenaHard, correlated with low perplexity (familiarity).

OpenHands (Apr 2025): a TRAINED critic lifts SWE-Bench Verified from 60.6% (single trajectory) to 66.4% (5 attempts), and the trained critic beats prompt-based reranking; DeepSWE 42.2%->59% and CWM 53.9%->65.8% with test-time scaling.
CrewAI task guardrails auto-retry the same agent up to ~2 additional times by default (configurable) — closest analog to the proposed design (docs.crewai.com).
LLM-judge cost per pass: ~$0.001-0.003 (GPT-4o-mini) or ~$0.015-0.045 (Claude Sonnet) — far below the $30-40/dev/mo willingness-to-pay for in-product reviewers (confident-ai.com).

In-product reviewer pricing: Cursor BugBot ~$40/mo add-on on a ~$20/mo base; Qodo ~$30/developer/mo. Devin: Pro $20/mo, Max $200/mo, Teams $80/mo, Enterprise historically ~$500/mo, billed by ACU compute.

Verifier reranking reaches higher accuracy at lower k than self-consistency using 1-3x fewer tokens; Self-Truncation Best-of-N matches full Best-of-N at 75-80% lower cost (openreview/Satori-SWE/SWE-Gym).

AI code-tools market ~$7.65B (2025) -> ~$9.46B (2026) at ~23.7% CAGR, ~$22.2B by 2030; AI code-review tool slice ~$750M (2025); ~46% of new code is AI-generated and ~40% of AI-generated code is reported to carry security vulnerabilities.

Rework rises 30-60% within 6 months of heavy AI tool adoption (for every 10 hrs saved, 4-6 go to rework); GitClear (211M LOC) found churn rose 5.5% (2020) -> ~7.9% (2024) and duplicated blocks rose ~8x; DORA 2024 estimated a 7.2% drop in delivery stability per 25% increase in AI adoption.

Security Degradation in Iterative AI Code Generation (arXiv:2506.11022): more refinement rounds accumulated MORE security vulnerabilities — direct evidence that unbounded auto-retry has downside risk, not just diminishing returns.

The verification verdict 'holds' only in the weak sense that 'some products sell critic-loop features'.

(arXiv:2406.01297) find no prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted-LLM self-feedback except exceptionally-suited tasks; Olausson et al. risks: Same-agent self-grading is biased: self-preference bias (arXiv:2410.21819) means a model over-rates its own buggy code, producing false 'pass' grades and missed defects. Mitigation: grader must be a distinct agent/context (atelier's reviewer/fixer split helps) AND grounded in external execution, not self-judgment.

Value-premise risk: a PURE self-grade loop is unlikely to improve quality and can degrade it (Huang et al.; CRITIC; Kamoi et al.). If the grade is not wired to real compile/test/lint signals, expect a multiplied token/latency bill (~Nx) for flat or negative accuracy.

Iteration risk: unbounded loops are an expensive, documented failure mode (Devin cost loops) and more rounds can accumulate security flaws (arXiv:2506.11022). Hard caps + convergence/state-hash dedup + an off-ramp are required, not optional.

Implementation risk: naively adding a grader step widens existing per-step limit duplication (4 copied max_agent_steps blocks) to a 5th/6th copy; and a new grade_round event is durably persisted but INVISIBLE in chat unless a projection arm is added (the step_limit_reached gap is precedent for silently-invisible events).

Schema risk: reusing AgentResult.status as pass/fail conflates 'agent finished' (NoChanges/ApprovalDenied) with 'work is correct'; a clean verdict needs a new field/schema and a synchronized update to all three runtime schema briefs (codex/claude/cursor).

Market/positioning risk: built-in self-correction is fast becoming table stakes (Claude Code 2.1 native auto-verification, Cursor, Devin, Cline). The loop alone is not a defensible USP; over-claiming 'unlocks what others paywall' is inaccurate and easy to refute.

Behavior-change risk: escalating exhausted cycles to the user via WaitingForUser is a change from today's hard-stop (RunState::LimitReached); the resume path only appends text + re-drives the orchestrator, so accept/retry/abort needs new selected_option_id routing in resolve_pending_clarification or it silently no-ops.

Budget-interaction risk: if a grader step consumes run.step_count like council does, a multi-round grade/retry sequence can exhaust max_agent_steps mid-loop and emit run_limit_reached before converging — the grader may need an off-budget or separately-capped accounting.
open_questions: Will the grade be grounded in external execution (run tests/lint via Capability::Command + RunCommand) or be a pure LLM self-grade? The evidence makes this the single most decisive design choice — external grounding is what works; self-grade alone is unreliable.

Mechanism choice: extend the EXISTING orchestrator-driven reviewer->fixer cycle (make the orchestrator auto-route reviewer after Edits) vs a NEW auto-injected grader sentinel force-injected at src/app/mod.rs:3083? These are distinct paths with different blast radius.

Grader identity: reuse the built-in reviewer profile, or a new grader sentinel modeled on council? If a sentinel, does it opt out of the council_route_allowed-style scope gate, and does it consume run.step_count budget?

Verdict contract: add a new structured verdict/score+critique field to AgentResult (and update the codex/claude/cursor schema briefs), or overload status+findings? A machine-parsable verdict is needed to gate retries deterministically.

surprises: Capability::Verify and Capability::Review are NON-gating: only Read/Command/Edit map to harness actions (src/config/mod.rs:64-71, src/actions/mod.rs:702-709). Verify/Review are pure routing/advisory signals, so a grader does not strictly need them to operate — it needs Read (and Command), and must lack Edit.
The Capability enum is in src/config/mod.rs:26-37, not src/actions/mod.rs as the idea hinted — actions/mod.rs only defines ActionKind/ToolName and the ActionKind->Capability mapping.

run_agent_step returns AgentStepOutcome::Completed even when the AgentResult.status is Blocked/Failed (src/app/mod.rs:3083-3094): step 'completion' means 'the agent produced a result', not 'the work succeeded'. Success/verdict lives in AgentResultStatus and ultimately in the orchestrator's DecisionStatus::Complete.

There is no independent machine verdict field at all — `verification` is the agent grading ITSELF (self-attested 'how I confirmed'), so it cannot serve as an external grader verdict; a grader would need a new field or to repurpose status+findings.

An existing reviewer profile + review_fix_cycle_count/max_review_fix_cycles already approximate a grader->fixer loop, but it is orchestrator-routed rather than auto-injected after an Edit-capable step; the idea's auto-grader would be a new force-inject at src/app/mod.rs:3083.

claims.claim: Event kinds are NOT a Rust enum — `HistoryEvent.kind` is a free-form `String`. There is no central kind registry; new kinds are added by simply passing a new string literal to `record_event`/`record_event_with_group`. (`AppEvent` at src/app/mod.rs:289 is unrelated — it is the TUI *input* event enum: PromptSubmitted/ApprovalAnswered/ClarificationAnswered/etc., not the durable event kind.)

claims.claim: `record_event` (src/app/mod.rs:4164) is a thin wrapper over `record_event_with_group` (4215-4241) which performs the full pipeline: build HistoryEvent::new_with_group, durable JSONL append (`history.append_event`), optional debug append, feed the chat projection (`chat_projection.apply_history_event`), `sync_chat_items`, push the human display string to `state.events`, and `publish_state` over the watch channel.
claims.evidence: src/app/mod.rs:4164-4173, 4215-4241; src/history/mod.rs:140-150 (append_event JSONL to .atelier/sessions/<id>/events.jsonl)

claims.claim: The durable schema is versioned by `schema_version` (always written as 1 at history/mod.rs:48); `read_events_from_path` hard-rejects any event with schema_version != 1 (history/mod.rs:274-280). Adding a new *kind* (not version) is forward-compatible: the projection's match has a catch-all `_ => {}` (projection.rs:110) so an unknown kind is persisted durably but silently ignored on render.
claims.evidence: src/history/mod.rs:48, 274-280; src/app/chat/projection.rs:59-111 (match with `_ => {}` at 110)

To make it visible in chat you must also add a consumer arm in `apply_history_event` (projection.rs:59) routing the kind to a new `apply_*` method — otherwise it is recorded but invisible. Other projections (e.g. `project_prompt_history`) filter on specific kinds and ignore it by default.

claims.claim: The chat projection collapses many events into one evolving item via `upsert` (projection.rs:1339-1383): each apply_* method emits an ItemInput carrying a `lifecycle_key: Option<ChatLifecycleKey>`. `upsert` derives the item id from the key; if `index: BTreeMap<ChatLifecycleKey,usize>` already holds that key it REPLACES the existing item in place (`*existing = ChatItemView{ source, ..item }`) while merging prior event_ids; otherwise it appends and records the index. Items with `lifecycle_key: None` get a `chat:event:<event_id>` fallback id and are never collapsed (always a new item).
claims.evidence: src/app/chat/projection.rs:23-30 (ChatProjection.index), 1339-1383 (upsert in-place replace + event_id merge); src/app/chat/mod.rs:206-229 (item_id per key)

claims.claim: `ChatLifecycleKey` (chat/mod.rs:117-144) has 7 variants — Prompt{run_id}, Run{run_id}, Clarification{run_id,question_id}, Workflow{run_id}, Step{run_id,step_id,item_kind}, Action{run_id,step_id,action_id}, FollowUp{follow_up_id}. The variant + its fields determine which events fuse into one item.
claims.evidence: src/app/chat/mod.rs:115-144

claims.claim: Clarification collapses to ONE evolving item: both `apply_clarification_requested` (projection.rs:1214) and `apply_clarification_answered` (1266) compute the SAME `Clarification{run_id,question_id}` key via `clarification_key` (1820, reads payload question_id), so the asked item (WaitingForUser) is upserted into the answered item (Completed). The answered arm even reads the prior item body through `self.index` to recover the question text (1273-1279).

Queued-follow-up collapses to ONE evolving item: `apply_follow_up_lifecycle` (projection.rs:1135) handles all five kinds (follow_up_queued/replay_started/replay_paused/replay_resumed/cancelled) all keyed by `FollowUp{follow_up_id}` from payload['id'] (1137), so a single item evolves Pending->Running->Paused->Pending->Skipped.
claims.evidence: src/app/chat/projection.rs:1135-1191; src/app/mod.rs:87-91 (kind routing list)

claims.claim: Council does NOT collapse into a single item. Each councillor result (councillor_result/councillor_agent_result/agent_result) is projected by `apply_agent_result` (885) keyed by `step_key` = `Step{run_id,step_id,AgentResult}` (1812), and councillors run as distinct steps -> one item per councillor. The council-level markers (council_started/council_synthesized/council_completed) route to `apply_diagnostic` (projection.rs:93-109) which sets `lifecycle_key: None` (1107) -> each is a separate keyless item, never fused.

Showing N grade/retry rounds as ONE evolving item needs: (a) a stable lifecycle key shared across rounds — a new variant e.g. `GradeCycle{run_id}` or reuse `Run{run_id}`; (b) an `apply_grade_round` arm that upserts that key, building cumulative body lines itself (upsert replaces in place, so the apply_* method must accumulate round history into the body, as apply_clarification_answered does by reading the prior item); (c) body is capped by `bounded_body`/MAX_BODY_LINES=12 so per-round lines must be compact; (d) to pin it chronologically at conclusion like run summaries, extend `is_terminal_run_conclusion` (1425) to recognize the new key+kind+terminal status.
claims.evidence: src/app/chat/projection.rs:19 (MAX_BODY_LINES=12), 1266-1300 (cumulative body via index read), 1339-1383 (in-place replace), 1421-1434 (is_terminal_run_conclusion)

claims.claim: The clarification pause is driven by the orchestrator returning `DecisionStatus::WaitingForUser` (orchestrator/mod.rs:43-48). The app's WaitingForUser arm (src/app/mod.rs:1895-1926) sets RunState::WaitingForUser, captures the FULL RunDriveContext via `pending_clarification = Some(PendingClarification{ run: run.clone() })`, mints a fresh question_id into a PendingClarificationView, records `clarification_requested`, and returns Ok(false) to stop the drive loop while RETAINING active_run_id.
claims.evidence: src/orchestrator/mod.rs:41-48; src/app/mod.rs:1895-1926, 366-369 (PendingClarification{run})

claims.claim: `drive_run` (src/app/mod.rs:1780-1800) treats WaitingForUser as suspension not conclusion: when WaitingForUser it deliberately skips recording workflow completion AND does NOT clear active_run_id, so the run stays alive and resumable.
claims.evidence: src/app/mod.rs:1780-1800 (guards `if !matches!(self.state.run_state, RunState::WaitingForUser)`)

claims.claim: `resolve_pending_clarification` (src/app/mod.rs:1689-1736) is the resume side: validates a clarification is pending and question_id matches (rejects mismatch/empty), `take()`s the captured RunDriveContext, records `clarification_answered`, then RESUMES by APPENDING the answer to the run prompt (`run.prompt = format!("{}\n\nUser clarification: {}", run.prompt, answer.answer)`), sets RunState::Planning, and calls `drive_and_replay(run, None)` which re-drives the SAME run through the orchestrator. There is NO branch that interprets the choice to abort/retry — the answer is just fed back as prompt text.

The clarification path IS a reusable pause/resume-to-user transport, and the TUI already supports option lists with a recommended default + free-text custom row, so accept/retry/abort can be modeled as three clarifying_options. BUT resume policy is fixed (answer appended to prompt + re-drive orchestrator); to make 'abort' actually stop or 'retry' re-run, the policy must be added either in the orchestrator (interpret the appended answer) or as a new selected_option_id branch inside resolve_pending_clarification. The transport (capture context, surface options, resume) is reusable as-is; the accept/retry/abort *decision routing* is not built in.
claims.evidence: src/app/mod.rs:1689-1736 (fixed resume = prompt append + re-drive); src/tui/mod.rs:2099-2176 (options + recommended + custom answer builder); src/orchestrator/mod.rs:64-66 (clarifying_question/clarifying_options fields)

claims.claim: There are TWO parallel escalation transports sharing the same skeleton (capture run context in a pending_* field, set WaitingForUser, retain active_run_id, record request event, on answer record resolved event + call drive_and_replay). Approval (resolve_pending_approval, 1587) is a BINARY y/n gate that resumes the EXACT paused step mid-flight via `StepResume{step:PausedStep, step_started_at, request:RuntimeRequest}` (728-746, 1680-1685). Clarification (resolve_pending_clarification, 1689) is a free-form/multi-option gate that resumes at the RUN level by re-driving the orchestrator. Both feed the follow-up queue pause path (`pause_oldest_pending_for_queue`; `queue_pause_reason` at 1400-1408 distinguishes waiting-for-approval vs waiting-for-clarification).
claims.evidence: src/app/mod.rs:727-746 (StepResume/PausedStep), 1587-1686 (resolve_pending_approval, StepResume resume), 1689-1736 (resolve_pending_clarification), 1395-1411 (queue_pause_reason)

Call `record_event(Some(run_id), step_id, "grade_round", json!({...round payload...}), "display")` from inside the run loop. It persists to JSONL, feeds the projection, syncs chat items, and publishes state. No enum to extend; payload is free-form JSON; schema_version stays 1.

integration_points.how: Add `"grade_round" | "retry_round" => self.apply_grade_round(event)` to make the new kind visible. Without an arm it falls through `_ => {}` and is recorded-but-invisible.

integration_points.name: ChatProjection::upsert + ChatLifecycleKey + index
integration_points.how: To render N rounds as one evolving item, give every round event the same lifecycle key (new `GradeCycle{run_id}` variant or reuse `Run{run_id}`). upsert replaces the keyed item in place and merges event_ids; the apply_* method must build cumulative body lines itself (read the prior item via self.index like apply_clarification_answered does). Mind MAX_BODY_LINES=12 (projection.rs:19).

integration_points.how: Extend to recognize the new key + RunSummary kind + terminal status so the concluded grade-cycle item is moved to the end (chronological) instead of staying pinned at its first-insert index.

integration_points.name: handle_orchestrator_decision WaitingForUser arm
integration_points.how: Reference template for surfacing an escalation: set RunState::WaitingForUser, store pending_clarification with the full RunDriveContext, build a PendingClarificationView with clarifying_options (e.g. accept/retry/abort) + recommended_option_id, record clarification_requested, return Ok(false). Reusable to escalate when grade cycles are exhausted.

integration_points.name: resolve_pending_clarification
integration_points.how: Resume side of the clarification transport. To turn it into an accept/retry/abort gate, add a branch on `answer.selected_option_id` BEFORE the prompt-append/re-drive (e.g. abort -> set Failed + record run_failed; retry -> reset cycle context + drive; accept -> Complete). Currently it only appends the answer to run.prompt and re-drives the orchestrator.

integration_points.name: resolve_pending_approval + StepResume/PausedStep
integration_points.how: The other (binary, step-level) escalation transport. Use as the model if a grade-cycle escalation needs to resume the EXACT paused step rather than re-drive the orchestrator; it carries RuntimeRequest + PausedStep through StepResume.

integration_points.name: review_fix_cycle limit stop site
integration_points.how: Where exhausted review/fix (grade) cycles currently hard-stop with RunState::LimitReached + run_limit_reached event. Replace/augment stop_for_review_fix_cycle_limit with a WaitingForUser clarification emission to escalate accept/retry/abort to the user instead of terminating.

surprises: Event 'kinds' are stringly-typed, not an enum — there is no compile-time registry. The de-facto registry of recognized kinds is the match in projection.rs:59-111; the producer side (src/app/mod.rs) and consumer side share no enforced enum, so a typo'd kind silently becomes an invisible (but durably persisted) event.

Council is the one multi-round case in the question that does NOT collapse into a single evolving item: councillor results are per-step items and the council_started/synthesized/completed markers are keyless diagnostics (lifecycle_key: None), so a council shows up as several separate chat items, not one.

Live agent-progress and the final agent-result are DIFFERENT chat items even for the same step: live steps key Step{...,AgentProgress} (transient, removed when the step leaves live_keys) while agent_result keys Step{...,AgentResult} (durable). The item_kind field is part of the lifecycle key, so progress vs result never fuse.

The clarification resume is implemented by literal string concatenation onto the run prompt ('\n\nUser clarification: <answer>') and a full orchestrator re-drive — there is no structured channel back into the run, so an accept/retry/abort gate built on it would rely on the orchestrator re-reading that appended text unless a selected_option_id branch is added in resolve_pending_clarification.

Two near-identical escalation transports already exist (approval = binary StepResume mid-step; clarification = option/free-form run re-drive). A grade-cycle escalation could reuse either, but neither currently routes a tri-state accept/retry/abort decision — that policy layer is absent.

Today exhausted grade cycles terminate with RunState::LimitReached (run_limit_reached, limit=max_review_fix_cycles) rather than asking the user anything, so adding user escalation is a behavior change at a single stop site (stop_for_review_fix_cycle_limit).

webFindings.angle: frameworks — The verify-and-retry / critic loop is NOT a paywalled differentiator: it is a documented, free PATTERN (Anthropic's evaluator-optimizer; the Reflexion / Self-Refine / CRITIC line of work) and a FREE framework primitive in every major open-source agent framework (LangGraph reflection/reflexion, CrewAI guardrails+retry, AutoGen/AG2 critic agent + nested chat + society-of-mind, OpenAI Agents SDK guardrails, Microsoft Agent Framework LLM-as-judge). The commercial autonomous coding products (Devin, Cursor) DO ship an automatic self-verify/fix loop, but they bundle it into a paid product and charge for the product/compute (Devin ACUs, Cursor Pro) — not for the critic loop as a separable SKU. So the idea's claim that 'a built-in critic loop is exactly the self-correction larger agent frameworks charge for' is largely FALSE/imprecise: OSS frameworks give the pattern away for free (you just assemble it), and paid products never itemize the loop. The harness's real, defensible differentiation is that the loop is AUTOMATIC-BY-DEFAULT and OPINIONATED (grader judges pass/fail, re-runs the SAME agent with the critique appended, bounded by max cycles) — convenience and being batteries-included, not unlocking something others gate behind a paywall. CrewAI's task-guardrail→auto-retry is the closest prior art and it is free/OSS. One nuance worth flagging: re-running the SAME implementer that was graded is a known weak spot; several systems (Claude Code's verification subagent, AG2's critic) deliberately use a SEPARATE/fresh model to grade so the worker isn't grading itself.

findings.claim: The verify-and-retry/critic loop is a documented, free PATTERN, not a proprietary capability anyone sells standalone
findings.detail: Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' describes the evaluator-optimizer workflow (one LLM generates, another evaluates and sends back specific feedback in a loop until a quality bar is met) and ships a runnable evaluator_optimizer.ipynb in the public cookbook. The academic lineage (Reflexion = learn via verbal self-feedback; Self-Refine = generate-critic-revise; CRITIC = tool-validated revision) is all open literature. Nobody monetizes 'a critic loop' as a SKU.

findings.claim: Every major open-source agent framework ships the critic/reflection loop as a FREE primitive you assemble yourself
findings.detail: LangGraph: reflection (generate->reflect->regenerate) and reflexion (tool-grounded critique + bounded revision via a conditional edge that returns 'continue'/'end'). AutoGen/AG2: a critic/reviewer AssistantAgent evaluates another agent's output and returns feedback; nested chats and SocietyOfMindAgent embed an inner critique monologue. Microsoft Agent Framework: LLM-as-judge implemented as another agent with a stricter rubric prompt. None of these charge for the pattern — the frameworks are OSS/free SDKs.
findings.source: langchain.com/blog/reflection-agents; docs.ag2.ai society_of_mind/nested-chat; techcommunity.microsoft.com Agent Framework LLM judge

findings.claim: CrewAI is the closest prior art to the proposed design and it is free/open-source
findings.detail: CrewAI task guardrails run immediately after an agent produces output, validate it (function-based or natural-language/LLM-powered), and on failure auto-route the error message back to the SAME agent to retry — with a configurable retry cap (docs/examples cite up to ~2 additional attempts). This is almost exactly the proposed 'grader judges pass/fail, re-run same agent with critique appended, bounded by max cycles', and it ships as a framework primitive with no upcharge.
findings.source: docs.crewai.com/en/concepts/tasks; analyticsvidhya.com CrewAI guardrails; github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI PR #1742

findings.claim: Commercial autonomous coding products bundle an automatic self-verify/fix loop, but charge for the PRODUCT/compute, not the loop as a line item
findings.detail: Devin spins up a VM, runs tests, reads error logs, and iterates/fixes autonomously (v3.0 adds dynamic re-planning) — and it is a paid product billed by ACU compute. Cursor's Agent mode runs a run-and-fix loop (runs tests/commands, watches output, iterates) with an opt-in lint-check setting, gated behind a paid Pro subscription. In both, the self-correction is included, never itemized as a premium 'critic loop' add-on.
findings.source: trickle.so/blog/devin-ai-review; docs.devin.ai/admin/billing; cursor.com test-generation; totalum.app Cursor Auto-review

findings.claim: ASSESSMENT of the idea's claim: 'a built-in critic loop is exactly the self-correction larger agent frameworks charge for' is largely FALSE / misleading
findings.detail: Two-part reality: (1) OSS frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen/AG2, MS Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK) give the loop away for free as a primitive — you pay nothing for the pattern, you just wire it. (2) Paid products (Devin, Cursor) bundle the loop into a whole agentic product and charge for product/compute, not for the loop itself. So no one 'charges for the critic loop' specifically. A more accurate positioning: the harness makes the loop AUTOMATIC-BY-DEFAULT and OPINIONATED — that is a convenience/UX differentiator (batteries-included), not access to a paywalled capability.
findings.source: synthesis across LangGraph/CrewAI/AG2/OpenAI/MS docs + Devin/Cursor pricing

findings.claim: OpenAI Agents SDK and MS Agent Framework split the concern: guardrails (safety/validation) vs LLM-as-judge (post-hoc grading) — neither is a same-agent retry-with-critique loop by default
findings.detail: OpenAI Agents SDK guardrails run input/output/tool validation in PARALLEL and fail-fast (more a safety tripwire than a regenerate loop); its eval/trace-grading lives on the paid OpenAI platform surface. Microsoft Agent Framework emphasizes post-execution LLM-as-judge rubric scoring. The proposed feature (grade -> re-run same agent with critique -> bounded cycles) is closer to CrewAI/Reflexion than to these.

findings.claim: Claude Code (the harness's direct competitor context) now ships native auto-verification plus subagent/hook-based grading
findings.detail: Claude Code 2.1 promotes auto-verification to a native workflow: generate code -> run lint/type/test -> evaluate against pass criteria -> self-correct and retry or confirm. Community patterns add a verification SUBAGENT (a fresh model tries to refute the result so the worker isn't grading itself) and Stop/PostToolUse hooks that gate task completion. This is bundled in the product, not an upcharge — and it means 'built-in self-correction' is becoming table stakes, not a unique selling point.
findings.source: sitepoint.com Claude Code 2.1 auto-verification; code.claude.com/docs best-practices; dev.to self-verification-loop

findings.claim: Bounding the cycle count is a validated, real need — unbounded self-correction loops are a known failure/cost mode
findings.detail: Devin users report the agent frequently 'gets stuck in expensive loops, racking up compute costs while failing to deliver working code.' LangGraph reflexion implementations make the max-cycle termination an explicit conditional edge. This supports the proposed design's 'bounded by a max cycle count' as the right guardrail rather than an afterthought.

findings.claim: Re-running the SAME agent that was graded is a deliberate design choice with a known weakness; some competitors use a separate/fresh grader
findings.detail: The proposed loop has a separate grader agent judge pass/fail, then re-runs the SAME implementer with the critique. Claude Code's verification subagent and AG2's critic intentionally use a SEPARATE (often fresh-context) model to grade so the producer isn't its own judge. Worth deciding explicitly: the harness already separates grader from implementer (good), but should ensure the grader is a distinct agent/context, not the implementer self-grading.

findings.claim: Self-reflection / verbal feedback loops measurably improve agent task success — BUT in the canonical papers the feedback signal is grounded in EXTERNAL outcomes (unit tests, environment rewards), not pure self-grade.
findings.detail: Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2303.11366) converts external feedback (test results, env reward) into verbal 'self-reflection' stored in memory and retried. It reports SOTA on code-gen (e.g. 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs 80% GPT-4 baseline in the paper) and an ~8% absolute boost from self-reflection over plain episodic memory. The authors explicitly note 'refinement-only approaches are not as effective as self-reflection-guided refinement' — i.e. the gain comes from grounding reflection in real signals. This is the strongest support for a verify-and-retry loop, with the caveat that the verifier is external (tests), not the model grading itself in a vacuum.
findings.source: Reflexion, Shinn et al. 2023, arXiv:2303.11366 (NeurIPS 2023); github.com/noahshinn/reflexion

findings.claim: Iterative self-feedback (Self-Refine) improves output quality across diverse tasks without any extra training — a direct precedent for a generate→critique→refine loop.
findings.detail: Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023, arXiv 2303.17651) uses the SAME model as generator, critic, and refiner. Across 7 tasks (dialog, math reasoning, code optimization, etc.) on GPT-3.5/ChatGPT/GPT-4, outputs improved ~20% (absolute, on their preference/quality metrics) vs single-pass generation. Key nuance the authors stress: 'specific, actionable feedback matters more than the number of refinement rounds' — vague self-critique adds little, and gains plateau quickly. This supports the loop but warns that loop quality hinges on critique specificity, not iteration count.

findings.claim: External tool/verifier feedback dramatically outperforms intrinsic self-evaluation — the model's own critiques contribute marginally and can be worse than the original answer.
findings.detail: CRITIC (Gou et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.11738) shows tool-interactive critiquing (code interpreter, search, calculators) is what drives correction. Their ablation: pure Self-Eval reaches only ~54% accuracy at verifying its own answers on HotpotQA (barely above random), and on TriviaQA self-critique performs WORSE than an 'only-true' baseline. Conclusion: 'the model's own critiques contribute marginally to improvement, and even fall short compared to the initial output.' Direct implication for a coding harness: tie the verify step to compiler/test/linter signals, not a self-grade.

findings.claim: COUNTER (the strongest): With no external feedback, LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning and performance can DEGRADE after self-correction — correct answers get changed to wrong ones.
findings.detail: Huang et al. 2023 ('LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet', arXiv 2310.01798, ICLR 2024) isolate 'intrinsic self-correction' (no oracle/external signal). On GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA, accuracy does not improve and often drops once the model is asked to review/revise — because it flips already-correct answers. They argue prior positive results leaned on oracle labels (knowing when to stop) that aren't available in deployment. This is the central risk for an automatic self-grade loop: false-negative self-grades trigger edits that break working code.

findings.claim: A critical meta-survey concludes self-correction via PROMPTED self-feedback essentially never works outside narrow, self-correction-friendly tasks; reliable gains require external feedback or large-scale fine-tuning.
findings.detail: Kamoi et al. 2024 ('When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes?', TACL 2024, arXiv 2406.01297) survey the field and find: (1) NO prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except tasks 'exceptionally suited' for it; (2) self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists (code interpreters, retrieval, oracle); (3) many positive papers used 'impractical frameworks or unfair evaluations that over-evaluate self-correction' (e.g. oracle stopping). This is the best single citation that a pure self-grade loop is unlikely to help and may be measuring an artifact.

findings.claim: FAILURE MODE — self-preference / self-evaluation bias: models systematically over-rate their OWN outputs, so a self-grader is a biased verifier prone to false 'pass' grades.
findings.detail: Wataoka et al. ('Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge', arXiv 2410.21819) quantify that LLMs, GPT-4 most strongly, rate their own generations higher than humans do. Mechanism: judges reward low-perplexity (familiar) text — the model finds its own output 'more predictable' and scores it up. Measured self-preference spans roughly -38% to +90% on ArenaHard. For a self-grading harness this is double-edged: it inflates pass grades on the model's own buggy code (missed defects) and, combined with verbosity/position bias, makes the grade an unreliable gate.
findings.source: Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge, Wataoka et al., arXiv:2410.21819

findings.claim: The error-localization bottleneck: LLMs are bad at FINDING their own mistakes even though they can FIX a mistake once its location is given — so the verify step, not the retry step, is the weak link.
findings.detail: Tyen et al. ('LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location', arXiv 2311.08516) decompose self-correction into mistake-finding vs output-correction. Models fail at mistake-finding (the verifier role) but succeed at correction once handed the location. Implication for a verify-and-retry loop: the value lives almost entirely in giving the loop an accurate, external locator (failing test name, stack trace, compiler error line) rather than asking the model to self-diagnose.

findings.claim: SUPPORT for a verifier (but a TRAINED/external one): test-time scaling with a dedicated critic/verifier model lifts coding-agent pass rates substantially — prompt-based self-reranking underperforms a trained critic.
findings.detail: OpenHands reported SOTA on SWE-Bench Verified by generating multiple rollouts and selecting with a trained critic model, improving from 60.6% (single trajectory) to 66.4% with five attempts; they explicitly found a trained critic beats prompt-based reranking. Broader test-time-scaling results (DeepSWE 42.2% pass@1 → 59% with TTS; CWM 53.9%→65.8% with TTS) confirm parallel-sample + verifier selection helps. Caveat for the harness: the lift comes from a SEPARATE verifier and best-of-N selection, not the same model self-grading a single attempt.
findings.source: OpenHands blog (Apr 2025) 'SOTA on SWE-Bench Verified with Inference-Time Scaling and Critic Model'; DeepSWE (together.ai); CWM arXiv:2510.02387

findings.claim: FAILURE MODE — iterative AI code generation can DEGRADE quality/security over passes, not just stall: more refinement rounds introduced more vulnerabilities in one systematic study.
findings.detail: 'Security Degradation in Iterative AI Code Generation' (arXiv 2506.11022) finds a paradox where repeatedly asking the model to expand/refine code accumulates security flaws across iterations. Combined with Huang et al.'s answer-flipping result, this is direct evidence that an unbounded auto-retry loop has downside risk, not just diminishing returns — argue for hard iteration caps and an external pass/fail gate before each retry.
findings.source: Security Degradation in Iterative AI Code Generation, arXiv:2506.11022

findings.claim: COST/LATENCY — multi-pass verify-and-retry multiplies tokens and wall-clock roughly linearly with passes; loops that don't gate on external signal pay this cost for near-zero accuracy gain (per Huang/Kamoi).
findings.detail: Self-Refine and Reflexion both run N full generate+critique+refine cycles, so cost and latency scale ~Nx the single-pass call (best-of-N verifier selection is even more, generating K parallel rollouts then scoring each). Because Huang et al. and Kamoi et al. show intrinsic (self-grade-only) loops yield little or negative accuracy, the expected ROI of a PURE self-grade loop is a multiplied bill for flat accuracy. The defensible design is: cheap external check (compile/test/lint) as the gate, capped retries, and reflection only on a real failure signal.
findings.source: Synthesis of Self-Refine (2303.17651), Reflexion (2303.11366), Huang et al. (2310.01798), Kamoi et al. (2406.01297)

findings.claim: Real-world AI-generated code already shows elevated defect/rework signatures, which is the practical problem a verify loop is meant to catch — but argues the gate should be tests/static analysis, the very signals that demonstrably work.
findings.detail: GitClear's analysis of ~211M lines (2025 report) found churn (code reverted/revised within two weeks) rose from 5.5% (2020) to a projected ~7.9% in 2024, copy/paste lines rose from 8.3% to 12.3% (+48% relative), duplicated code blocks rose ~8x, and refactored ('moved') lines fell from 24.1% to 9.5%. Cloned code is associated with 15-50% more defects in cited research. Google DORA 2024 estimated a 7.2% drop in delivery stability per 25% increase in AI adoption. These motivate an automated verifier but point it at external quality signals, not self-grading.
findings.source: GitClear 2025 AI Copilot Code Quality report; Google DORA 2024 report (via GitClear/DevOps.com summaries)

findings.claim: AI code review / verification is a distinct, fast-growing market segment with strong demand signals, not just a feature
findings.detail: The broader AI code-tools market is sized at ~$7.65B (2025) growing to ~$9.46B (2026) at ~23.7% CAGR (reaching ~$22.2B by 2030). The narrower AI-code-review tooling slice is estimated at ~$750M in 2025. Pure-play AI code-review vendor ARR is reported at ~$420M for 2026, up from ~$180M in 2025 (~133% YoY). Search demand for 'AI code review' reportedly grew +310% from mid-2025 to Q1 2026, and Gartner is cited estimating 30% of enterprises with 1,000+ developers had deployed at least one AI code review tool by end of 2025. Demand is driven by the fact that ~46% of new code is now AI-generated, which turns human-only review into a bottleneck.

findings.claim: The cost of low-quality AI-generated code is large, measurable, and concentrated in rework/defects — the core pain a self-grading critic targets
findings.detail: Engineering leaders analyzing post-AI metrics report rework rates (developer time spent fixing recently-shipped code) rising 30-60% within six months of heavy AI tool adoption; one widely-cited framing is that for every 10 hours saved by AI code generation, 4-6 hours go to rework, debugging, and incident response. Translated to budgets, a $1M AI development project implies ~$300K in unplanned rework. Quality data backs the pain: SonarSource's Aug-2025 analysis found a 'systemic lack of security awareness' in LLM output, ~40% of AI-generated code is reported to carry security vulnerabilities, and GitClear's analysis of 211M lines found duplicated code blocks rose 8x in 2024 while refactoring dropped to historic lows. Macro anchor: CISQ estimates poor software quality cost the US economy ~$2.41 trillion, dominated by rework.

findings.claim: Automated grading/verification (LLM-as-judge / verifier) is already productized and monetized along two distinct lines
findings.detail: Line 1 — eval/judge platforms sold to AI builders: DeepEval/Confident AI, Braintrust, Galileo, Evidently (OSS lib >25M downloads + cloud), LangSmith, Arize, and Ragas all ship LLM-as-judge scoring as a product. Line 2 — in-product agent reviewers/verifiers sold to developers: Cursor BugBot, Qodo (PR review + Qodo Cover test-gen), Greptile, and autonomous agents like Devin that 'iterate until they reach a result for review.' This confirms both 'judge-as-a-service' and 'verification-as-a-paid-feature' business models exist; a self-grading critic loop sits at their intersection (an internal verifier rather than a separate SKU).

findings.claim: Pricing signals: graders bundle cheap; in-product reviewers command a $30-40/dev/month premium
findings.detail: Eval/judge platforms anchor low per-seat (DeepEval: $0 Developer / $39 seat/mo Plus / custom Enterprise). In-product reviewers price higher and as add-ons: Cursor BugBot is ~$40/month on top of Cursor's $20 base; Qodo is ~$30/developer/month positioned as the premium 'quality platform.' The raw token cost of a single LLM-judge pass is small — roughly $0.001-0.003 with GPT-4o-mini and $0.015-0.045 with Claude Sonnet — meaning the willingness-to-pay ($30-40/mo) vastly exceeds marginal grader compute, so a per-step grader is economically defensible if it demonstrably cuts rework.

findings.claim: Research validates that verifier-based reranking / per-step grading buys quality at acceptable, tunable cost — the central cost-latency argument for a per-step grader
findings.detail: Test-time-scaling literature shows verifier reranking reaches higher accuracy at lower k than self-consistency while using 1-3x fewer tokens, and Self-Truncation Best-of-N matches full Best-of-N at 75-80% lower cost. The cost curve is steep and tunable: Best@50 can match SOTA while Best@500 costs >10x; simple non-agentic pipelines hit 27.3% solve at just $0.34/issue. This supports framing a grader as 'cheap insurance' — a single verification pass per step is a small token multiplier on the actor, and aggressive sampling is optional, not required.

findings.claim: Multi-pass critic loops are an established pattern, but the dominant design risk is the 'self-confirmation / hallucination barrier' — the angle that differentiates a credible grader
findings.detail: Reflexion (actor/evaluator/self-reflection) and actor-critic adversarial coding are well-documented patterns; loops typically run 3-5 rounds until the critic approves or a max-iteration cap hits, and are reported to cut downstream human review cycles from 3-5 to 1-2. The critical caveat: when the verifier is the same model critiquing itself, the system only works if the critic interface induces stricter evaluation than the actor — otherwise it sits near the 'hallucination barrier' and self-confirms. Practical safeguards required: max-iteration limits, tracking whether cycles actually improve metrics, and state-hash dedup to prevent infinite/non-converging loops. This means a trustworthy self-grader needs structural rigor (rubric, separate framing, objective checks), not just 'ask the model if it's happy.'

findings.claim: User expectations: developers tolerate added latency/cost only when it is bounded and visibly reduces rework; uncapped loops are the failure mode
findings.detail: The market framing favors 'spend extra compute only when reliability matters' — single-model quick polishing for simple tasks, multi-agent reflection reserved for complex/high-reliability work. Buyers already pay premiums (BugBot autofix spawns cloud VMs; Qodo runs pre-merge gates), indicating tolerance for background/async verification cost. But the cited risks (infinite reflection loops, non-converging cycles) mean users expect hard caps, convergence tracking, and an off-ramp. For a per-step grader, the defensible framing is: bounded passes (e.g., cap at N), a small token multiplier per step vs. the actor, and an explicit 'this caught X before you had to review it' value story tied to the 30-60% rework figures.

verdicts.evidence: The core mechanism is confirmed. A reserved id constant `pub const COUNCIL_WORKFLOW_AGENT_ID: &str = "council"` (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:9) acts as the sentinel id. It is resolved as a virtual routing target in `validate_agent_reference` (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:642-653), which special-cases the id and bypasses the real `config.agents.get(agent_id)` lookup (line 654), returning Ok without a configured agent; validation is reached via `validate_decision_next_step` (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:486,500,558) and it gets a synthetic routing line in `build_orchestrator_prompt` (src/orchestrator/mod.rs:704). Dispatch happens in the drive loop: `drive_and_replay` (src/app/mod.rs:1286) -> `handle_single_agent_decision` (src/app/mod.rs:1886,1954) -> `if next_agent_id == COUNCIL_WORKFLOW_AGENT_ID` at src/app/mod.rs:1960 calls `run_council_workflow` (src/app/mod.rs:3155). Synthesis is `synthesize_council_decision` at src/app/mod.rs:5557. Both workflow execution and synthesis live in app/mod.rs, matching the claim.
verdicts.correction: Three precision caveats. (1) The code never calls it a "sentinel"; it is named COUNCIL_WORKFLOW_AGENT_ID / "harness workflow" — "sentinel" is an apt paraphrase, not a literal term. (2) The claim's phrasing implies dispatch is in the orchestrator module and only synthesis in app/mod.rs, but the orchestrator module (src/orchestrator/mod.rs) only VALIDATES the virtual target and emits the prompt routing line; the actual dispatch (src/app/mod.rs:1960), workflow execution (src/app/mod.rs:3155), and synthesis (src/app/mod.rs:5557) ALL live in app/mod.rs's drive loop. So "inside the orchestrator decision loop" only holds if "orchestrator decision loop" means the OrchestratorDecision-processing drive loop in app/mod.rs, not code under src/orchestrator/. (3) There is NO generic virtual-target registry: council is the only such target, wired through hardcoded `if agent_id == COUNCIL_WORKFLOW_AGENT_ID` string-equality branches at 3 sites (orchestrator/mod.rs:642, app/mod.rs:1960, and the prompt line orchestrator/mod.rs:704). A "grader sentinel" would copy this shape (new const + validation branch + dispatch branch + prompt line + workflow/synthesis fns), i.e. a parallel bespoke path following the same template — not plug into an extension point. So "clean reuse rather than a bespoke path" is aspirational; the council path is itself bespoke.

verdicts.claim: AgentResult already exposes verification/findings/blocker that a grader could emit a structured verdict through, AND the clarification WaitingForUser pause/resume can carry the escalation when cycles are exhausted.
verdicts.evidence:
Part 1 (fields exist): src/orchestrator/mod.rs:147-160 defines `struct AgentResult` with `findings: Vec<String>` (line 154), `verification: Vec<String>` (line 157), `blocker: Option<String>` (line 158), alongside `status: AgentResultStatus` (line 152) and `summary` (line 153). AgentResult is the structured agent-step output contract: `RunStepResult::Agent { result: AgentResult }` (line 165), and `AgentResult::completed` initializes these fields empty (lines 224-240). So a grader agent could populate findings/verification/blocker to emit a structured verdict. No grader exists yet (grep for `grader`/`grade`/`verdict` finds only unrelated symlink-resolution `verdict` usages in src/actions/mod.rs:672,687), so this is a feasibility claim about existing fields, which holds.

Part 2 (WaitingForUser is a real generic pause/resume that can carry an escalation): Orchestrator emits `DecisionStatus::WaitingForUser` carrying `clarifying_question` + structured `clarifying_options` (id/label/description) + `recommended_option_id` + `multi_select` — src/orchestrator/mod.rs:64-73, 78-83, validated at 404-416/447-469. App pauses on it: `RunState::WaitingForUser`, stores `PendingClarification { run }`, surfaces `PendingClarificationView`, records `clarification_requested` — src/app/mod.rs:1895-1925. Resume: `resolve_pending_clarification` appends the user answer to the run prompt, sets `RunState::Planning`, and re-drives the same run — src/app/mod.rs:1689-1736. verdicts.correction: Both halves are accurate only as feasibility/capability claims ("could emit"/"can carry") about existing primitives — NOT as descriptions of existing wiring. Two gaps to flag: (1) No grader/verdict-emitting agent exists today; the three AgentResult fields are present but nothing currently writes a structured verdict into them. (2) The "when cycles are exhausted" path is NOT currently routed through WaitingForUser. When `max_review_fix_cycles` (default 2, src/config/mod.rs:178,190) is reached, the app calls `stop_for_review_fix_cycle_limit`, which sets `RunState::LimitReached` and records a `run_limit_reached` event (src/app/mod.rs:1977-1980, 1993-1998, 3704-3724) — it terminates the run rather than escalating to the user via clarification. So escalating exhausted cycles through the WaitingForUser clarification flow is a feasible reuse of the existing pause/resume primitive, but it would require new wiring; today exhaustion dead-ends in LimitReached.

verdicts.claim: Automatic self-critique/reflection loops materially and reliably improve coding-agent output quality (the feature's core value premise).
verdicts.evidence: The literature splits on one decisive axis — whether the loop is grounded in EXTERNAL feedback (test/compiler/linter execution) or is pure intrinsic self-grade. SUPPORT (external-feedback case): Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023) reports +11 pts pass@1 on HumanEval and SOTA code-gen results, but it consumes external signals (unit-test results, environment feedback) — https://openreview.net/pdf?id=vAElhFcKW6 . Self-Refine (Madaan et al.) shows iterative refinement gains across tasks. 2025 studies (Stanford test-runner-feedback work; "How Many Tries Does It Take?", https://arxiv.org/html/2604.10508) find execution-feedback self-repair materially improves code/test generation, and newer 2024-2025 models repair more reliably. REFUTE/CAVEAT (pure self-critique): Huang et al., ICLR 2024 "LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798) finds intrinsic self-correction WITHOUT external feedback fails and performance sometimes DEGRADES, and that earlier reported gains often relied on oracle labels. Olausson et al., ICLR 2024 "Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?" (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.09896) finds gains are modest/variable/sometimes absent once repair cost is counted, and that self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's own feedback quality — a human expert's feedback yielded 1.58x more passing fixes than GPT-4's self-feedback. Self-preference bias work (NeurIPS 2024, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.13076 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21819) shows LLM judges favor their own generations, with harmful bias worst exactly when the model is weak on that instance — undermining the self-grading half of any pure reflection loop. So "material" improvement is well-supported when loops are grounded in external/test feedback, but "reliably" as an unqualified universal is contested: pure automatic self-critique is unreliable and can reduce quality.
verdicts.correction: Qualify the premise: self-critique/reflection loops materially and reliably improve coding-agent output ONLY when grounded in EXTERNAL feedback (running tests, compiler/linter/traceback signals, or oracle stopping criteria). The improvement is driven by that external signal, not by the model's self-assessment. Pure intrinsic self-grade is the weak link — it is unreliable (self-preference bias), is bottlenecked by the model's ability to localize its own errors, and can degrade output (Huang et al.; Olausson et al.). For the feature to deliver its value premise, the reflection loop must be wired to execute tests/tools and feed real results back, not merely ask the model to re-grade itself; expect diminishing or negative returns from ungrounded self-critique, especially on weaker models, and budget for the extra inference cost which can erase modest gains.

verdicts.claim: Major agent frameworks/products ship an automatic critic/verifier loop as a notable, sometimes paid/premium capability — supporting the idea that this is "what larger frameworks charge for".
verdicts.evidence: The descriptive core is well-supported. The critic/verify-refine loop is a productized pattern across major frameworks: LangChain/LangGraph ship a reflection pattern (langgraph-reflection: main agent -> critic/judge -> loop), and AutoGen and CrewAI support coder+critic reflection loops. It is grounded in established methods — Reflexion (arXiv 2303.11366), Self-Refine (arXiv 2303.17651, NeurIPS 2023; ~20% preference gain), and CRITIC. The 'sometimes paid/premium' qualifier is concretely true: Cursor BugBot positions its review-to-fix loop as a premium feature (8 parallel passes + majority voting + validator; BugBot Autofix spawns cloud agents; pricing moved from $40/seat to usage-based ~$1.00-1.50/review), CodeRabbit is a widely adopted paid AI-review product (2M+ repos, 13M+ PRs), and OpenAI o1/o3 internalize verifier/process-reward models as a premium reasoning tier. Sources: LangGraph reflection (vijaykumarkartha.medium.com/self-reflecting-ai-agents-using-langchain-d3a93684da92); Self-Refine (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651); BugBot/CodeRabbit pricing (https://aicodereview.cc/tool/cursor-bugbot/, https://www.devtoolsacademy.com/blog/state-of-ai-code-review-tools-2025/); o1 verifiers (https://openai.com/index/deliberative-alignment/).
verdicts.correction: Two important caveats temper the rhetorical conclusion. (1) External feedback matters far more than pure self-grading: Huang et al., 'LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet' (ICLR 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798) found LLMs fail to self-correct reasoning without external feedback and can DEGRADE after intrinsic self-correction; self-preference bias (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21819) shows LLM judges favor their own outputs even when objectively worse (plus verbosity/position bias). Effective critic loops therefore rely on asymmetric/external signals — a different model, passing tests, tool/search results, or user clarification — not a model grading itself. (2) The phrase 'what larger frameworks charge for' overstates exclusivity: the critic/verifier loop itself is commoditized and freely available in open-source frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, public Reflexion/Self-Refine). Paid products (BugBot, CodeRabbit, Qodo, LangSmith) monetize the surrounding packaging — cloud compute, autofix, ensemble validation with a real validator, integrations, observability — rather than the loop as a uniquely gated primitive. So the claim is best read as 'some products sell critic/verify-loop features,' not 'the loop is what frameworks fundamentally charge for.'
